newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: El Nino raises Indonesia 1998 coffee crop concerns.
newsitem.headline: El Nino raises Indonesia 1998 coffee crop concerns.

text.p: A dry spell, believed to have been triggered by the El Nino weather pattern, is beginning to bite on Indonesian coffee farms and may disrupt the current flowering for next year's crop, traders said on Wednesday.

"It's very dry, much drier than is normally the case this time of the year. The effects of El Nino are starting to hit. If you don't have any rains and the coffee trees are flowering, it may affect production," a veteran coffee dealer told Reuters.
Another dealer said several Indonesian coffee farms "have got emergency irrigation. But this dry spell is going to do some harm somewhere."

El Nino, named after the Christ child by Peruvian fishermen to describe the phenomenon of unusually warm Pacific Ocean temperatures off the coast of South America, normally peaks around December and can affect weather patterns worldwide.

Meteorologists have warned this year's El Nino may have arrived early and could match the century's worst in 1982-1983, which blighted crops in Indonesia, Australia, the Philippines and southern Africa with a blistering drought.
Floods ravaged India, Peru and Chile, severe winter storms pounded California and record snowfalls piled up in the Rocky Mountains of North America.

One trader said next year's possible fall in coffee output in Indonesia, the world's third leading coffee producer behind Brazil and Colombia, may be even more drastic than the 20-25 percent drop expected in the 1997 crop.
"The fall in Indonesia's production next season may even be more severe because of this El Nino," he said.
Indonesia is the world's largest producer of the robusta grade of coffee and its harvet runs between April and September.
Robusta coffee is more bitter in taste than higher grade arabica coffee, which is predominantly grown in Central and South America, but also in East Africa and India.
In contrast to its regional competitor, Vietnam is said to be getting adequate rainfall and its 1997/98 crop appears to be coming along nicely, dealers said.

London robusta prices are tipped to bounce back later on Wednesday after hovering yesterday at six month lows. The September contract tumbled to a six-month low of US$1,477 a tonne before closing $42 down on the day at $1,505.
"There will be a bounce. By the numbers, it should be $100 up. I'm calling it $50 higher," one trader said. Another dealer said a recovery of between $20-$30 is more likely.

Overall, Southeast Asian coffee trade was quiet with the region's currency woes not seen as affecting business. Trade houses have begun making offers for Vietnamese robusta coffee, but no deals were concluded, traders said.

"I think some of the smaller Indonesian exporters may be affected (by the regional currency crisis), but the big exporters deal in (U.S.) dollars and get their loans in dollars. The impact should be minimal," one said.

The Indonesian rupiah has been hammered by speculative attacks over the past week. It slipped back again on Wednesday after the Thai baht sanked to fresh lows. The Indonesian unit was quoted at 2,570/600 to the dollar at 0425 GMT.
Regional dealers said routine offers for Vietnam's Grade 2 coffee, 8.0 percent black and broken, have been made.
"I'm also offering," one dealer said, adding though that no deals appear to have been concluded so far.
"The European houses are trying to make some offers for Vietnam's Grade 2 at $150 under (basis) September London for October/November shipment," another trader said.
Dealers said the range of offers for Vietnamese coffee was seen at $150-$250 under the close on Tuesday of London's September robusta contract.

Some contract wash-outs from Indonesia were also seen by dealers and said this was expected after prices dived from their peak level last May of US$2,700 a tonne on the London robusta market. Indonesian grade 4 export robusta was indicated at $1,430/$1,505 a tonne FOB Lampung on Wednesday.
"There have been some non-performance of contracts, but that is expected with prices at these levels," a trader said.
Business remained slow with most of the roasters from the U.S. and Europe away for the summer holiday season.
"It's quiet on both sides," a dealer said.
"I have not seen any business coming out of Indonesia," a coffee analyst added.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
